findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the SIGTERM stub's post-signal behavior (e.g. signal the script then exit non-zero without reading or recording a successful write, or signal the process group) and assert the expected rc 143 deterministically, with a bounded test timeout.

'Each case asserts a non-zero exit, the "already replaced" / "SSM was NOT" / "cannot authenticate" notice on stderr'
findings.finding: The SIGTERM test case ('`aws` sends SIGTERM to the script mid-write') does not specify what the stub does after sending the signal. Bash defers the script's TERM trap until the stub exits. If the stub then exits 0, the case actually models 'SSM write succeeded, then the signal was handled'. Asserting the 'SSM was NOT updated' notice there locks in a false statement. If the stub blocks or sleeps, the test may hang or become timing-dependent. The case also does not model a real Ctrl-C, where the whole process group (including `aws`) is signalled.
findings.location: Testing — third parametrized case: '`aws` sends SIGTERM to the script mid-write (interrupted operator run)'
scenarios: The stub kills $PPID and then exits 0. The test passes while asserting a notice that is false for that sequence of events.
The stub kills $PPID and then sleeps. The script waits on the child, and the test is slow or flaky.

findings.finding: The EXIT trap is armed before `--delete-token default`. If the delete call itself fails (for example an ssh error or a Gerrit rejection), the trap still prints 'Gerrit's token ... was already replaced', which may be false: the old token can still be intact. This contradicts the AC, which limits the notice to failures 'after deleting'.
findings.location: Approach: 'Just before the `--delete-token default` call (the point of no return) arm an `EXIT` trap'

findings.suggested_fix: Arm the EXIT and signal traps on the line immediately after `--delete-token default` returns successfully. Alternatively, have the trap print a hedged 'token may have been deleted' message while a DELETED flag is still unset.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the notice truthful across the whole trap window: either word it conditionally ('may have been replaced / may not have been updated') or arm it after the delete succeeds; also handle the deferred-signal-after-successful-put case, and state the chosen behavior for a failing `--delete-token` call.

AC: 'When `service-user.sh` fails at any step after deleting the bot's `default` token and before the SSM write succeeds'
Bash semantics: a trap for a caught signal is not executed until the current foreground command completes.
findings.finding: The trap window does not match the facts the notice asserts. (a) The EXIT trap is armed 'just before the `--delete-token default` call'. If that ssh call itself fails (connection refused, auth failure), the script exits under the trap. The operator is then told 'Gerrit's token ... was already replaced' and 'the review-bot cannot authenticate', even though the token may never have been deleted. (b) Bash defers a trapped SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP until the running foreground command (`aws ssm put-parameter`) returns. If the put succeeds and the signal arrived during it, the TERM trap runs before the planned `trap - EXIT INT TERM HUP`. It exits 143 and prints 'SSM was NOT updated' when SSM was in fact updated. The AC scopes the notice to failures 'after deleting the bot's default token and before the SSM write succeeds', but the mechanism fires outside that window too.
findings.location: Approach — 'Just before the `--delete-token default` call (the point of no return) arm an `EXIT` trap' / 'Disarm all four ... immediately after `aws ssm put-parameter` succeeds'
scenarios: ssh to Gerrit fails on the delete call. The operator is told the bot is locked out when nothing changed, and may escalate or rotate unnecessarily.
An operator presses Ctrl-C while `aws ssm put-parameter` is completing successfully. The notice claims SSM was NOT updated, contradicting the real state.
findings.suggested_fix: Word the notice as uncertain state with a clear recovery: 'Gerrit's token for <bot> may already have been replaced and SSM may not have been updated; the review-bot may be unable to authenticate until this script succeeds — re-run it.' Alternatively, keep the categorical wording but arm the EXIT trap only after `--delete-token` returns 0, and accept or document the delete-time signal gap. Add a test case for a failing delete call that asserts the chosen behavior.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the post-delete notice accurate when the delete itself may not have happened: arm the trap only once the delete has succeeded, or record the delete's exit status and have the notice say the token "may have been" replaced when that status is unknown.

Plan notice text: "Gerrit's token for '<bot>' was already replaced and SSM was NOT updated; the review-bot cannot authenticate"
findings.finding: The traps are armed before a delete call that hides its own failure (`2>/dev/null || true`), and the notice states as fact that "Gerrit's token ... was already replaced". If Gerrit cannot be reached, the delete fails silently and the generator then exits non-zero. The new trap would then wrongly tell the operator that the review-bot is locked out, even though its token was never changed. Today the script exits with no message in this case. Under the plan it would print a false alarm.
findings.location: Approach — "Just before the `--delete-token default` call (the point of no return) arm an `EXIT` trap that prints the notice"
scenarios: The operator runs a rotation with the VPN off or a stale admin key: both ssh calls fail, and the script reports that the bot is locked out when it is not.
A SIGTERM arrives after `aws ssm put-parameter` has written the value but before the stub or process returns: the script says "SSM was NOT updated" when SSM was updated.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the delete's outcome, e.g. `if $GERRIT_SSH gerrit set-account "$BOT_USER" --delete-token default 2>/dev/null; then deleted=1; else deleted=0; fi`. Arm the traps before this call so a signal during the delete is still caught. Have the EXIT trap print the definite "was already replaced" wording only when the token is known to have changed, i.e. `deleted=1` or the generator has returned. Otherwise print a hedged "may have been replaced; re-run this script" line. Add an "ssh unreachable" test case that asserts the definite wording is absent.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Account for Bash holding trapped signals until a foreground command finishes: say in the plan and the notice text what happens when a signal arrives during a successful `aws ssm put-parameter`, and pin the SIGTERM test stub's exit status (non-zero after sending the signal) so the test exercises an interrupted write.
evidence: Plan: "plus `INT`/`TERM`/`HUP` traps that `exit 130/143/129` so a signal also exits non-zero and runs the `EXIT` trap. Disarm all four (`trap - EXIT INT TERM HUP`) immediately after `aws ssm put-parameter` succeeds"
Plan Testing: "`aws` sends SIGTERM to the script mid-write (interrupted operator run)". The stub's own exit status after sending the signal is not specified.
Bash manual (Signals): "If Bash is waiting for a command to complete and receives a signal for which a trap has been set, it will not execute the trap until the command completes."
service-user.sh lines 77-82 run `aws` as a foreground pipeline stage under `set -euo pipefail`, so a TERM sent with `kill` from another terminal while it runs is held until `aws` exits.
findings.finding: The plan assumes that a TERM/INT/HUP trap runs as soon as the signal arrives during the `aws ssm put-parameter` call. Bash actually holds a trapped signal until the foreground command finishes. If a SIGTERM reaches the script while `aws` is running and `aws` then succeeds, the TERM trap runs after the successful put but before `trap - EXIT INT TERM HUP`, so the script exits 143 and prints 'SSM was NOT updated' even though SSM now holds the new token. The SIGTERM test case ('aws sends SIGTERM to the script mid-write') also never says what exit status the stub returns after sending the signal, so it is not pinned whether the test covers the 'aws failed' case or this false-notice case.
findings.location: Approach ("INT/TERM/HUP traps that exit 130/143/129 so a signal also exits non-zero and runs the EXIT trap"); Testing (SIGTERM case); infra/gerrit/service-user.sh lines 77-83
scenarios: An operator runs `kill -TERM <script pid>` while `aws ssm put-parameter` is in flight. `aws` is not in the signalled process and finishes successfully, writing the new token to SSM. Bash then runs the TERM trap, exits 143, and the EXIT trap prints 'SSM was NOT updated; the review-bot cannot authenticate'. The operator is told the opposite of what happened and may re-run, deleting a token that was working.
The test stub sends SIGTERM and then exits 0. The script still exits 143 with the notice, so the test passes, but it is really testing the false-notice case rather than an interrupted write.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach, add one sentence: a TERM/INT/HUP that arrives while `aws` is running is handled only after `aws` exits, so the trap may fire after a successful put. Either word the signal-path notice as 'SSM may NOT have been updated' (keep the exact wording for the set -e failure paths), or have the signal trap record the signal and make the EXIT handler check whether the put already returned 0. In Testing, have the SIGTERM stub send the signal and then exit non-zero (for example 143), and optionally add a case where it signals and exits 0 to cover the chosen behaviour.

findings.finding: The SIGTERM fixture is under-specified. Bash defers a trap until the foreground child exits, so the `aws` stub must send the signal to the script's PID and then exit; if it signals and then blocks, the test hangs. The plan also does not say how the stub obtains the script's PID: `$PPID` is wrong if `aws` runs inside a command substitution or subshell.

scenarios: The stub kills a subshell instead of the script, so the test asserts against an ordinary aws failure rather than a signal.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the per-arm disposition: the trap preserves each step's original exit status (1/254/143/1), and every post-delete failure is retryable by re-running the script. Assert the exact rc per parametrized case rather than just non-zero.
evidence: 'Each case asserts a non-zero exit'
Root cause lists the distinct rcs: 'rc 1, 254, 143'
Notice text: 'cannot authenticate until this script succeeds' (implies re-run, but no explicit disposition word)
findings.finding: The failure-disposition contract is stated only as 'non-zero exit'. The plan does not say that the EXIT trap preserves the underlying exit status (1 from the generator, 254 from aws, 143 from the signal, 1 from the shape-check). It also does not explicitly label the post-delete failure state's disposition, i.e. that re-running the script is the safe, retryable remedy rather than something needing manual Gerrit/SSM repair. The tests assert only 'a non-zero exit', so a trap that clobbered $? (e.g. with a trailing command or `exit 1`) would still pass.
findings.location: Approach / Testing — 'Each case asserts a non-zero exit'
scenarios: An operator wrapper or runbook keys on exit 254 (AWS credential problem) versus 1 (Gerrit problem). A trap that normalizes the status hides which leg failed.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach, add: 'The EXIT trap captures rc=$? first, prints the notice, and exits with the same rc; every arm is retryable by re-running the script after fixing the cause (AWS session, Gerrit reachability).' In Testing, assert rc == 1 / 254 / 143 for the three cases.
